title: Plan 9 from Outer Space

evidence.note: The Public Domain Review catalogs the film under 1959 and lists the underlying work's rights status as 'PD U.S.', but it cites no registration or renewal search, and it marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'. A web search summary attributed to the AFI catalog says the film was not registered for copyright at release and that Reynolds Pictures, Inc. registered a videocassette version on April 23, 1981. We could not open the AFI page (it returned HTTP 403), so we could not confirm this. We also could not search the Copyright Office catalog for registration or renewal records in this session. Because no primary record was checked, this layer stays undetermined.

Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Parts 12-13: Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan-Dec 1958 (archive.org identifier catalogofcopyrig3121213li). We confirmed the volume's title and year on its archive.org page. We did not search its text for this film, so it does not settle the question.
evidence.source: Internet Archive / Library of Congress Copyright Office

evidence.note: The soundtrack follows the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer). The music was compiled by Gordon Zahler from stock recordings of works by about a dozen composers, according to Wikipedia's article on the film. Each of those compositions and recordings may have its own copyright history. Check each one before licensing it for new synchronization or commercial release.

Ed Wood is credited as producer, writer, director and editor of the film in the Internet Archive item description. We found nothing showing it was adapted from an earlier published work, so the story takes the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer).

USPTO trademark databases could not be searched automatically in this session. We know of no active mark for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space', but trademark status stays undetermined until a USPTO search is done.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions such as a new score, colorization, or new titles and subtitles can be protected. A colorized version of the film circulates on the Internet Archive, and any such colorization can carry its own protection. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Plan 9 from Outer Space is a science-fiction horror film that Ed Wood produced, wrote, directed and edited. Reynolds Pictures, Inc. made it. Wikipedia reports that it was shot in black and white in November 1956 and previewed at the Carlton Theatre in Los Angeles on March 15, 1957. Distributors Corporation of America released it nationally in July 1958. It is known for its cult reputation as one of the 'worst films ever made'. The Public Domain Review catalogs it under 1959 and lists the underlying work's rights status as 'PD U.S.', but it cites no registration or renewal search and marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'.

The rights trap is that nobody has shown the status with a primary record. A web search summary attributed to the AFI catalog says the film was not registered at release and that a videocassette version was registered by Reynolds Pictures, Inc. in 1981. We could not open that page or search the Copyright Office catalog ourselves. The soundtrack is also a compilation of stock recordings of works by about a dozen composers, and each of those may have its own history. Treat the film as unverified until a registration and renewal search is done, and get advice before reusing footage commercially.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.', but cites no registration or renewal search, and we could not run one. The status is undetermined until a Copyright Office search is done. Get advice before reusing footage commercially.
Does an Internet Archive copy or a Creative Commons label mean I can reuse it?

No. A hosting label on an uploaded copy does not decide the film's copyright status. The Public Domain Review marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear', and any added material such as a new score, colorization or new titles can be protected on its own.
